newsitem.title: USA: Crucial to keep inflation down, Greenspan says.
newsitem.headline: Crucial to keep inflation down, Greenspan says.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said Tuesday that it was crucial to keep inflation down in the short run to help keep the economy purring.
In prepared testimony to the House Budget Committee, Greenspan said that low inflation and inflation expectations have been a major reason why the economy has performed so well over the past year.
"Consequently, it is crucial to keep inflation contained in the near term and ultimately to move toward price stability," Greenspan said.
He said that America's ecomomic performace over the past year has been "quite favorable," with few signs of the imbalances that might have been expected this late in an economic expansion.
"The most likely prospect," he added, "is for continued sustainable economic growth accompanied by low and stable inflation."
Greenspan spent the bulk of his prepared testimony repeating his past argument that the consumer price index over states inflation and should be fixed.

As he has done before, Greenspan called for the establishment of an independent national commission to set annual cost-of-living adjustments for federal government taxes and spending programs, including social security.
Such a move would presumably save the government billions of dollars each year, but would mean lower benefits than otherwise for the elderly and other recipients of governmemt programs.
Greenspan also urged Congress to provide the government's Bureau of Labor Statistics with enough money to vigorously address problems with the CPI that tend to inflate it.
He estimated, as he has in the past, that the upward bias on the CPI ranged from between 1/2 to 1-1/2 percentage points per year.
Greenspan said that virtually all components that make up the CPI are approximations, "in some cases, very rough approximations."

While calling for additional financial support for government statisticians to help improve the accuracy of the CPI, he said, "Some upward bias will almost surely remain in the CPI, at least for the next several years."

He said the bottom line was that the best available evidence suggests that the United States was overcompensating the average social security recipient for increases in the cost of living, while at the same time the adjustment is causing the inflation-adjusted burden of the income tax system to decline more rapidly "than I presume the Congress intends."
